title: Coherent extrapolated volition
html:
I read two emotionally heavy pieces today:

  1. On the alignment of Machines and Men - Julia Willemyns
  2. The silent consensus - Dean Ball

This is a walk through what I feel after reading all three. I write this scared -- for I think there's no way I have a voice that'll be heard. Very few people are going to take decisions that change my life, and the life of the people I love. 

Premise: It's clear that we'll hit a version of RSI/AGI in the next 3 years, with a real chance that this process will lead to lives negatively affected. A lot of the US economy already rests on AI leading to more profits. The pressure to keep going is immense. 

1. Alignment of machines and men

The author points at how human societies regularly change the way they think about morality and justice: 

  • Systems like hue and cry had to be phased out because they were impractical with economic realities. The plague displaced a lot of human labor and there just wasn't a lot of humans around to hunt down a fleeing thief.
  • Japan's Koban model had to be phased out because of a declining population. The nature of crime itself changes too. 
  • The US has a system of social control that relies on insurers, landlords, private companies and public institutions, civil society, and independent courts. The US system values individual liberty, and at the same time tries to prevent bad behavior.  There's no one policing every move an individual takes. This comes with a cost, of course. 
  • China, on the other hand, relies on prevention. They focus on surveillance of the public as much as possible. Individual liberty is definitely not as valuable here as it is in the western liberal democracies. 
  • The larger point is: both are equally valid systems. But beneath them is a normative choice. The choice of valuing personal liberty, or the party's principles. 

The author seems to be mentioning all this in opposition of this idea of perfect alignment. Can perfect alignment exist when we have constantly evolved our notion of justice? We need the freedom to evolve our definition of justice. Morals are very subjective however contradictory that might read. A lot of mentions of violence that has existed in our shared history. A testament to our capability to do bad stuff. I genuinely don't see the point of invoking these feelings here though. I do see the point that we have come a far way, and even though our history is full of violence and suffering, we have endured. We have in effect created a benevolent society using a wide range of social pressures. 

We need the freedom to evolve our system whenever we want. The idea of perfect alignment is very authoritarian. I strongly think the author is strawmanning "perfect alignment". I haven't heard of anyone arguing for "perfect alignment." That's why I'm taking the larger vibe the author seems to be going for -- CEV.

Coherent extrapolated volition -- that all-encompassing term. To me, CEV is something like: "You get the goodness vibe going around right now? Don't change the goodness vibe. Extrapolate everything else." 

I'm unable to give any more thoughts on CEV. It's about trusting your successor (the AGI) enough that they'll take care of you, I guess? I also fear of how this might mean that AGI will just throw us into a hedonistic simulation. The author rightfully invokes the Wall-E chair in the end. 

We seem to want to instruct our models this: "Take care of us, make sure we live, and make sure we're happy." Then the AGI will come up with the best solution. It'll plug us up to a never ending game of pleasure. 

2.  The silent consensus 

The author here invokes the image of them looking at their child. They're scared of telling their kid that decisions will be taken for them. They'll get the plushiest passenger seat in the car. They could ask for the seat to be made as luxurious as possible. But the author only wants this: the kid on the wheel. Nothing other than the kid on the wheel is acceptable. 

Invoking the looming disempowerment is the best thing you can do to remind people of the risks of RSI and AGI. I think people have a hard time imagining how an AI could actually kill them. "Just turn of the thing," one can always say. Ok, but our capitalistic societies simply don't allow for this turning off. A capitalistic and individualistic person, who the author is, has all the reason to keep this machines going, because they will drive profits further more than any other team of competent humans. 

I think the most powerful idea here for me is the author's struggle here: 

We will have to swim against the current of economics, and in so doing, reject many of the things that are dogma for classical liberal individualists like me. This will be a perilous endeavor, one in which failure is far from improbable. But if this is not a fight worth having, no fight is worth having. 

The whole essay feels very political. The struggle between what the author truly believes in as a member of a capitalist society, and what the technology seems to be serving us, create a tension that makes the author question, and question harder. 

Democracy means that everyone has a seat at the table. It's that simple. I don't have to get eliminated because my neighbour is better than me. I have a right to exist. Similarly, there should be no reason for an AI to not treat us as their equal, even though they're destined to be vastly more capable than we are. The author expresses a hope that the future AGI truly believes in this. They look at the world as a thing they share with everyone else. (Our record as humans is not stellar regarding this but we're trying.) 

The silent consensus, according to the author, is that we're all set to lose human primacy. 

I like how the author points out the coping sentence: "AI is just a tool." It's cope because by saying this, we're not simply declaring our hope in a human-led future. We're actually refusing to do equal work to accept the potential of superintelligence. I think this was crucial to point out. 

Well, in the end, it's upon us to preserve our primacy. The author stresses on how it was us who have emerged from the mud. Feels like a very Christian/Western way of looking at things? I personally don't feel like I carry the legacy of my ancestors. Because I think this link is then never ending. If the primacy has its origins in the humans inventing the fire, then the apes who ventured out into the savannah are more deserving of that primacy. I think this chain never ends, and if you want to invoke the legacy to justify your primacy, I feel it's wrong. I can't quite point out why. I don't agree with this framing at all. (I will try to make a better effort in arguing why at some other time.)

For it is we who came up out of the mud. We who forged primitive society out of dirt and stone. We who gazed up at the stars and asked why. We, with our fighting and our love and our envy and our joy, who discovered morality and ethics and law. It is we who sang and danced, wrote and composed. It is we who made history, and it is we who wrote it. That legacy is ours. The civilization we have built is a flame we have tended, and that flame belongs to us. Our past is a glorious inheritance over which we all are stewards, and part of that stewardship is our participation in what Michael Oakeshott called “the conversation of mankind,” that grand endeavor that began in primeval times.

Why say this? Ugh. 

Anyway, I get it. We should be in the steering wheel and we need to be considered an equal when sitting at the table along with superintelligence. [Even though we're not arguably treating other members of planet earth the same, we should expect superintelligence to be truly benevolent, sentient and god-like and keep us on the table because you know what, humans are special, other living things are not]. I'm sure but this essay is full of contradictions for me. I get that the author is arguing that we will have to fight for a future that is human. YES! But our track record is really bad. I don't see how this essay has added value to my way of thinking. Do we expect that we'll magically teach superintelligence to value us? Will we build institutions that let us be equal? More questions than answers. The silent consensus exists because our own record speaks for itself and it's inevitable; but now that you are at stake, you suddenly want to declare yourself as special? Why? Do we think chicken wouldn't have wanted an equal say in everything too? Aren't we to ants as we are to superintelligence? That's the go-to analogy afaik. Do we care about ants? The answer to this should be a natural response to the silent consensus. 

At the end, I know the author is not pointing at this. They stress on how agents should be tethered to their humans. If we ever allow independent agents, that should come with very heavy guardrails. This message is actually hopeful. If we don't allow agents to rummage through everything will value, we might save ourselves from irrelevance, or at worst, we will get more time before this happens.

I know I may have misread many many things. This is what I truly felt upon reading and I will be wrong here. I want to get better at this kind of a thing anyway.

Rather than consuming stuff and not talking about it, the point was to consume and make the experience count. I don't want to think "Oh I read those two pieces that day. People write such cool stuff" and then let it go. This is a part of an effort to be more intentional with my time and the words I read.
